## Definition

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite positive measure, let $h:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$ be a measurable statistic. For $\eta\in\mathbb R^k$ put

$$Z(\eta)=\int h(x)e^{\eta\cdot T(x)}\,\mu(dx),\qquad H=\{\eta:0<Z(\eta)<\infty\},\qquad A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta).$$

For a parameter set $\Omega\subseteq H$, the associated **exponential family** has laws $P_\eta$ with density

$$p_\eta(x)=h(x)\exp\{\eta\cdot T(x)-A(\eta)\}\quad(\eta\in\Omega).$$

The normalization $A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta)$ makes each density integrate to one. In this item **full-rank** means that $\Omega$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$ and there do not exist $b\ne0$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ with $b\cdot T=c$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{h>0\}$. A parameter set containing an open subset is also called regular in some sources; terminology varies, so this definition controls here. The condition is stronger than needed for the completeness theorem below but rules out redundant displayed coordinates.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

A **finite-group randomization setup** consists of a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ as in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], a finite group $G$ acting on $\Omega$ as in [[def-group-action]], a statistic $T:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and a family $\mathcal P_0$ of null probability laws on $\Omega$ that is invariant under the action. Invariance means that for every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $g\in G$, and $A\subseteq\Omega$, $P(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P(A)$. The **orbit** of $x$ is $O(x):=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$, a finite subset of $\Omega$. The setup itself does not assert that the action is free or that distinct group elements give distinct orbit points.

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. For
$0\le t\le T$, let
$(E_t,\mathcal E_t)$ be a standard-Borel state space; for $1\le t\le T$, let
$(F_t,\mathcal F_t)$ be a standard-Borel observation space
([[def-standard-borel-space]]), meaning a measurable space bimeasurably
isomorphic to a Polish space. A probability kernel has probability-measure
sections and measurable evaluations as in
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Specify an initial probability
measure $\mu_0$ on $E_0$ (a measure of total mass one, as in
[[def-probability-measure]]), transition probability kernels $K_t$ from
$E_{t-1}$ to $E_t$, and observation probability kernels $G_t$ from $E_t$ to
$F_t$, for $1\le t\le T$.

The trajectory space, with the finite product sigma-algebra generated by
measurable coordinate rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]), is
$$\mathcal Z_T=E_0\times E_1\times F_1\times\cdots\times E_T\times F_T,$$
with $\mathcal Z_0=E_0$. Its finite-horizon law $P_T$ is the unique probability
law whose ordered iterated kernel integral is
$$\mu_0(dx_0)\prod_{t=1}^T K_t(x_{t-1},dx_t)G_t(x_t,dy_t).$$
The product notation means successive integration in the displayed order; it
does not assert the existence of densities. Existence and uniqueness under AC
are proved in [[thm-finite-horizon-state-space-kernel-law-exists-uniquely]].
Every finite product trajectory space is standard Borel by
[[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]].

The initial and transition laws specify the state evolution, while each
$G_t$ specifies the observation law given the current state in this model.
State evolution by itself therefore does not specify a joint state-observation
law. No density or time-homogeneity assumption is imposed, and no strict
stationarity assumption (shift invariance of all finite-dimensional laws) is
required ([[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]]). This is a
single law, not a parameter-indexed family. The model contract records a
proposed law and makes no claim that it adequately describes an application
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
and define the full replacement $X_{t,0}=f(\delta'_{t,0,t},\delta'_{t,0,t-1},\ldots)$. Each $X_{t,m}$ has the same marginal law as $X_t$; for fixed $m\ge1$ the sequence $(X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary and $m$-dependent because its original-innovation windows have length $m$ and its replacement arrays are independent across $t$.

For every fixed $m\ge0$, the joint process $(X_t,X_{t,m})_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is strictly stationary: shifting all indices relabels a family of mutually independent innovations with the same law and commutes with the defining measurable maps. Consequently $D_{t,m}:=X_t-X_{t,m}$ is stationary and $\|D_{t,m}\|_{L^2(H)}=\delta_m$ for every $t$.

Write $\|X\|_{L^2(H)}=(\mathbb E\|X\|_H^2)^{1/2}$ and
$$\delta_m=\|X_0-X_{0,m}\|_{L^2(H)},\qquad m\ge0.$$
The process is **$L^2$-$m$-approximable** when
$$\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2<\infty\qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\sum_{m\ge1}\delta_m<\infty.$$
The same marginal law gives $\delta_0\le2\|X_0\|_{L^2(H)}<\infty$. For a Bochner-integrable $H$-valued random element $Y$, write $\mathbb E_B Y=\int Y\,d\mathbb P$; the moment condition makes $X_t$ and every $X_{t,m}$ Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]], [[thm-bochner-integrability-criterion]]).

Here **strict stationarity** means invariance of every finite-dimensional law under integer shifts. A process is **$m$-dependent** if, for every $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(X_s)_{s\le a}$ and $(X_s)_{s\ge a+m+1}$ are independent ([[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]). The stated input windows for $X_{t,m}$ are disjoint across these two index ranges, so they satisfy this definition.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$. Let
the state dimension at time
$t$ be a positive integer $d_t$ for $0\le t\le T$, and the observation
dimension at time $t$ be a positive integer $p_t$ for $1\le t\le T$.
Choose deterministic matrices
$F_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_{t-1}}$ and
$H_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times d_t}$, a mean $m_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}$, and
symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices, meaning $v^TPv\ge0$ for every
real vector $v$ of matching dimension,
$P_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0\times d_0}$,
$Q_t\in\mathbb R^{d_t\times d_t}$, and
$R_t\in\mathbb R^{p_t\times p_t}$. A **linear-Gaussian state-space model
with independent noises** is the general finite-horizon kernel model
([[def-general-state-space-model-by-kernels]]) with initial law
$\mu_0=N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$ and transition and observation kernels
$$K_t(x,\cdot)=N_{d_t}(F_t x,Q_t),\qquad G_t(x,\cdot)=N_{p_t}(H_t x,R_t).$$
All Gaussian laws use the convention of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]], which allows singular covariance matrices.

Its independent-noise representation consists of random vectors
$x_0,q_1,r_1,\ldots,q_T,r_T$ on a common probability space, with
$x_0\sim N_{d_0}(m_0,P_0)$, $q_t\sim N_{d_t}(0,Q_t)$,
$r_t\sim N_{p_t}(0,R_t)$, all mutually independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]] (their generated sigma-algebras are
independent), and equations
$$x_t=F_t x_{t-1}+q_t,\qquad y_t=H_t x_t+r_t\qquad(1\le t\le T).$$
The local path-law theorem proves that every allowed parameter tuple has
such a finite representation, that its induced kernels are the displayed
$K_t,G_t$, and that its path law is the general kernel-product law.

This definition imposes the stated noise law and independence assumptions;
it does not establish their empirical adequacy. It supplies no filtering
algorithm, posterior recursion, or convergence claim. Any separate formula
that inverts an observed innovation covariance must assume that covariance is
positive definite at the point of inversion.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, meaning a set with
a specified sigma-algebra ([[def-measurable-space]]), and let
$L:\Theta\times\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$ be a loss function whose section
$a\mapsto L(\theta,a)$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable for each $\theta$. A
randomized decision rule is a probability kernel $\delta$ from the data space
to the action space ([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its
**risk** at $\theta$ is the extended nonnegative number
$$R(\theta,\delta)=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}L(\theta,a)\,\delta(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
The inner integral is a measurable function of $x$, by
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], so the outer nonnegative integral
is defined by [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].
A deterministic measurable rule is included by taking its point-mass action
kernel. No measurability on $\Theta$ is required for this definition.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

For a finite-group randomization setup with statistic $T$, the **inclusive orbit upper-tail rank** at $x\in\Omega$ is
$$p_0(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the observed data and uniform on $[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized orbit rank** is
$$p_U(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Both counts are over group elements, with multiplicity. Thus a nonfree action counts a distinct orbit point as many times as it has preimages under $g\mapsto g\cdot x$.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Suppose an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ also has a measurable
parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A
**Markov kernel** (or **probability kernel**) representation is a function
$$
K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]
$$
such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, the set function
$A\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
and, for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and every Borel set $C\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$
\{\theta\in\Theta:K(\theta,A)\in C\}\in\mathcal T.
$$
Here the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,1]$ is generated by its relatively open
subsets $U\cap[0,1]$, where $U$ is open in $\mathbb R$. Thus the second
condition says that each event-probability map $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,A)$ is
measurable. The kernel represents the given experiment exactly when
$K(\theta,A)=P_\theta(A)$ for every $\theta$ and $A$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-probability-measure]]).

This is an optional parameter-measurable version of a model. An arbitrary
experiment does not include a measurable structure on $\Theta$ or imply this
kernel condition.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.
After observing $x$, the procedure assigns probability $K(x,B)$ to taking an
action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

A **randomized test** is a randomized procedure with binary action space
whose action set is $\{0,1\}$, equipped with its full sigma-algebra
$2^{\{0,1\}}$ (the power set, which is a sigma-algebra by
[[def-sigma-algebra]]), where $1$ means reject and $0$ means do not reject
([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its **test function** is
$$\varphi(x)=K(x,\{1\}),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.$$
Since $K(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure and $\{0\},\{1\}$ partition the
action set, $K(x,\{0\})+K(x,\{1\})=1$. Thus $\varphi(x)\in[0,1]$ and
$1-\varphi(x)=K(x,\{0\})$ is the probability of not rejecting. Give $[0,1]$
the trace of the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,+\infty]$, namely
$\{C\cap[0,1]:C\in\mathcal B([0,+\infty])\}$. By
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], $x\mapsto K(x,\{1\})$ is
measurable; since it has range in $[0,1]$, its preimage of $C\cap[0,1]$ equals
its preimage of $C$ and is measurable for every such $C$. Hence $\varphi$ is a
measurable map in the preimage sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Its value is the
rejection probability after observing $x$.
The convention $1=\text{reject}$ is fixed here. No null or alternative
hypothesis is part of this definition.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Definition

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge0$ be finite integers, and let $(Y_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered strictly stationary sequence of $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|Y_0\|^2<\infty$. Strict stationarity means that every finite-dimensional law is invariant under integer shifts. Assume $m$-dependence: for each $a\in\mathbb Z$, the sigma-algebras generated by $(Y_t)_{t\le a}$ and $(Y_t)_{t\ge a+m+1}$ are independent, in the sense of [[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]. Set
$$\Sigma_m=\sum_{|j|\le m}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_j),$$
where $\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)=\mathbb E[(U-\mathbb EU)(V-\mathbb EV)^T]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Then $\Sigma_m$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and
$$\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\ \Rightarrow\ N_d(0,\Sigma_m).$$
The conclusion allows singular $\Sigma_m$, including $\Sigma_m=0$.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$,
let $(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered causal Bernoulli shift as in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], and suppose it is
$L^2$-$m$-approximable. Write $\sigma=(\mathbb E\|X_0\|_H^2)^{1/2}$,
let $S_1(H)$ be the trace-class Banach space with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]),
write $\mathbb E_B$ for a Bochner integral, and define $x\otimes y:H\to H$ by
$(x\otimes y)h=\langle h,y\rangle_Hx$. The Bochner series
$$ \Gamma=\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_0]+ \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\bigl(\mathbb E_B[X_0\otimes X_j] +\mathbb E_B[X_j\otimes X_0]\bigr) $$
converges absolutely in trace norm to a positive self-adjoint trace-class
operator. For $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$, the Bochner covariance operators
$\Gamma_n=n^{-1}\mathbb E_B[S_n\otimes S_n]$ satisfy
$\|\Gamma_n-\Gamma\|_1\to0$. If $\boxtimes$ is the product-kernel class from
[[lem-real-l-two-kernel-operator-is-bounded-and-rank-one-compatible]], then
$$ \kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_0\boxtimes X_j],\qquad \widetilde\kappa_j=\mathbb E_B[X_j\boxtimes X_0] $$
are well-defined elements of $K=L^2([0,1]^2,dt\times dt;\mathbb R)$, and
$$ c=\kappa_0+\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(\kappa_j+\widetilde\kappa_j) $$
converges absolutely in $K$ and satisfies $T_c=\Gamma$. Equivalently, $c$ is
the design's long-run covariance-kernel series interpreted as an
$L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class; no pointwise representatives are fixed.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let $\Gamma:H\to H$ be positive, self-adjoint and trace class. Then there is a Borel $H$-valued random element $G$ such that every $\langle G,h\rangle_H$ is a centered real normal random variable and
$$\mathbb E[\langle G,h\rangle_H\langle G,k\rangle_H]=\langle\Gamma h,k\rangle_H\qquad(h,k\in H).$$
This is the centered Gaussian law with covariance operator $\Gamma$; it includes finite-rank and zero covariance.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

In a finite-group randomization setup, fix a null law invariant under the group action. Conditional on every orbit $O$ with positive probability, the data are uniform on the distinct points of $O$. For the orbit ranks of [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]], the inclusive p-value $p_0$ is superuniform under the null, and the independent-uniform tie-randomized value $p_U$ is Uniform$(0,1)$ conditionally on each positive-probability orbit. Consequently, $p_U$ is also Uniform$(0,1)$ unconditionally.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Let $d,k\ge1$, let $r_n>0$ be deterministic with $r_n\to\infty$, and let $T_n$ be $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with target $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Suppose $Z_n=r_n(T_n-\theta)\Rightarrow Z$ for an $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector $Z$. All vector norms below are Euclidean.

If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ is Borel and there is a linear map $A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$g(\theta+h)-g(\theta)=Ah+\rho_1(h),\qquad \frac{\|\rho_1(h)\|}{\|h\|}\longrightarrow0\quad(h\to0,\ h\ne0),$$
then
$$r_n\{g(T_n)-g(\theta)\}\Rightarrow AZ.$$

If, in addition, $A=0$ and there is a continuous symmetric bilinear map $H:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$g(\theta+h)-g(\theta)=\frac12H[h,h]+\rho_2(h),\qquad \frac{\|\rho_2(h)\|}{\|h\|^2}\longrightarrow0\quad(h\to0,\ h\ne0),$$
then
$$r_n^2\{g(T_n)-g(\theta)\}\Rightarrow \frac12H[Z,Z].$$
For scalar-valued $g$, $H$ is the usual Hessian bilinear form. The second-order premise is a pointwise Peano expansion; continuous second derivatives on a neighborhood are not required.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(P_\eta)_{\eta\in\Omega}$ be the exponential family of [[def-exponential-family]] on a standard Borel sample space, with $\Omega\ne\varnothing$, and let $T$ be its canonical statistic. Then $T$ is sufficient.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H=L^2([0,1],dt;\mathbb R)$ and let
$(X_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ be a centered, $L^2$-$m$-approximable causal
Bernoulli shift as defined in
[[def-l2-m-approximable-causal-bernoulli-shift]], with Bochner mean
$\mathbb E_BX_0=0$. Let $\Gamma$ be its long-run covariance operator from
[[lem-long-run-covariance-is-trace-class]], and let $G$ be a centered
$H$-valued Gaussian random element with covariance $\Gamma$, whose existence
is given by [[lem-positive-trace-class-covariance-defines-hilbert-gaussian]].
Then, for $S_n=\sum_{t=1}^nX_t$,
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\ \Rightarrow\ G$$
in the weak topology of Borel probability measures on $H$. The covariance
kernel is the $L^2([0,1]^2)$ equivalence class $c$ in the long-run covariance
lemma, and its integral operator is $T_c=\Gamma$. This is a CLT for the
$H$-valued sample sums; it is not a functional CLT for the time-indexed
partial-sum process.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ be an estimand, and set
$\mathcal M:=\mathsf P(\Theta)$, the set of laws in the model. For
$\theta\in\Theta$, write
$$
[\theta]_\sim:=\{\eta\in\Theta:\eta\sim\theta\}.
$$
Then the following are equivalent: **(i)** $\psi$ is identifiable; **(ii)**
$\psi$ is constant on every observational equivalence class $[\theta]_\sim$;
and **(iii)** there is a unique function $\bar\psi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal T_0$
such that $\psi=\bar\psi\circ\mathsf P$.

The factorization is a statement about sets and functions. It asserts no
measurable structure or measurable factor map.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
satisfies
$$P_\theta(p(X)\le\alpha)=E_\theta[\varphi_\alpha(X)]\le\alpha \qquad(\theta\in\Theta_0).$$
Consequently, whenever a nonempty alternative hypothesis
$\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$ is specified, this test has size
at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$ in the sense of
[[def-test-size-and-power]].
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Assume AC. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one measurable space, with
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A}|P(A)-Q(A)|,$$
the event-supremum convention without a factor $1/2$,
$$\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}\le\sqrt{\frac12D(P\|Q)}.$$
If $P\not\ll Q$, the right side is $+\infty$ by the definition of KL
divergence.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\subseteq
\mathbb R^d\}$ be dominated by a common sigma-finite measure, with $\Theta$
open, and suppose the model is QMD at an interior $\theta_0$ with score $s$
and information $I=E_{\theta_0}[ss^T]$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID
$P_{\theta_0}$, and for each fixed local sequence $h_n\to h$ set
$u_n=h_n/\sqrt n$. Then the local product laws
$P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}$ admit mean-one likelihood-ratio proxies
$L_n$ relative to $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$ such that
$$\left\|P_{\theta_0+u_n}^{\otimes n}-L_nP_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}\right\|_{\rm TV} \to0,$$
and under $P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}$,
$$\log L_n=h_n^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_P(1),\qquad \Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns(X_i)\Rightarrow N_d(0,I).$$
Thus the IID QMD experiment is LAN in the proxy sense of
[[def-lan-experiment]]. This assertion does not claim that the full local
product law has a Radon–Nikodym derivative relative to the base law.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law
$P_{\theta_0}$ in a dominated parametric model
$\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$, where $\Theta$ is open in $\mathbb R^d$,
$d\ge1$, and $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Let $p_\theta$ be densities with respect
to one supplied sigma-finite measure. Suppose the model is QMD at $\theta_0$
with score $s_{\theta_0}$ and positive-definite information
$I=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$. Assume there are a
neighborhood $V$ of $\theta_0$ and a nonnegative measurable $L$ with
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}L^2<\infty$ such that, on one $P_{\theta_0}$-full set,
$$
|\log p_{\theta_1}(x)-\log p_{\theta_2}(x)|\le L(x)\|\theta_1-\theta_2\| \qquad(\theta_1,\theta_2\in V).
$$
Suppose a measurable exact MLE $\hat\theta_n$ exists and is consistent, in
the sense that $P_{\theta_0}(\|\hat\theta_n-\theta_0\|>\varepsilon)\to0$
for every $\varepsilon>0$. Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=I^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n s_{\theta_0}(X_i)+o_{P_{\theta_0}}(1)\ \Rightarrow\ N_d(0,I^{-1}).$$
Under the same local hypotheses, every consistent measurable exact likelihood
maximizer over a possibly $n$-dependent subset that contains $\theta_0$ is
also root-$n$ bounded in probability.
The conclusion is asymptotic; it gives no exact finite-sample normal law.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Let $d,k,m\ge1$ be fixed. For each $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y_n\in\mathbb R^k$ be random vectors on one probability space; the probability space may vary with $n$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ be a random vector on any probability space, and let $c\in\mathbb R^k$ be constant. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n-c=o_P(1)$, then
$$ (X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c). $$
Consequently, for every continuous $h:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R^m$, $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$. No independence between $X_n$ and $Y_n$ is required.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

resolved_external_interfaces.interface_text:
## Statement

Let all random vectors with index $n$ be defined on a common probability space for that $n$; the spaces may vary with $n$. In any fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the following rules hold:

1. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=o_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=o_P(1)$. If $U_n=O_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=O_P(1)$.
2. For positive integers $p,q,r$, let $B:\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^r$ be a fixed map for which there is a constant $C\ge0$ with $\|B(u,v)\|_2\le C\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ for all $u,v$. Assume in each application that $B(U_n,V_n)$ is a random vector on the same probability space as $U_n,V_n$, for every $n$. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, or conversely, then $B(U_n,V_n)=o_P(1)$. If both are $O_P(1)$, then $B(U_n,V_n)=O_P(1)$.
3. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ in $\mathbb R^d$, then $X_n=O_P(1)$.

The last conclusion is finite-dimensional boundedness in probability. No independence or Axiom of Choice is assumed.
resolved_external_interfaces.review_scope: Statement/Definition compatibility only; no new proof audit or acceptance claimed

contract_boundary_notes: BCS-01/02 and likelihood consumers: statistical-experiment and likelihood-density supply neither parameter sigma-algebra nor parameter/joint measurability. Use the exact parameter-measurable kernel supplier and explicitly impose jointly measurable dominated density as already planned.
BCS-07/08/09/15/19/20: KL has its published direction and AC premise; Pinsker uses event-supremum TV, natural log and TV <= sqrt(D(P||Q)/2).

BCS-10: QMD implies proxy LAN, not blanket local absolute continuity. MLE supplier requires correct specification, QMD, positive-definite information, L2 log-likelihood Lipschitz envelope on a common full set, and consistent measurable exact MLE. Posterior normality/tail control remains BCS-local.

BCS-03/24/59: exponential-family normalization and sufficiency are for the published standard-Borel, sigma-finite model; sufficiency assumes AC. No arbitrary-summary sufficiency or positive-tolerance ABC theorem is imported.

BCS-38/39: SME-44 supplies finite-horizon standard-Borel kernel models under AC. Linear Gaussian state/noise covariance may be singular; every innovation inverse needs its separate SPD premise. No filtering or convergence theorem is imported.

BCS-50: MSF-36 uses H=L2([0,1]), centered L2-m-approximable Bernoulli shifts, and a sample-sum Hilbert CLT. It is not a time-indexed partial-sum FCLT or a bootstrap-validity result. Block-bootstrap validity remains local.

BCS-51/52: the MSF-11 finite-group supplier has a finite sample space and invariant null law, with orbit uniformity on distinct orbit points. General measurable-space or asymptotic permutation validity remains local.
